summary: Provides a framework for using Path Computation Elements to do inter-layer traffic engineering in MPLS and GMPLS networks. It looks at optimizing resources across all layers together rather than separately. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A large network often runs on top of a smaller one, such as internet traffic carried over an optical backbone. Planning each layer on its own wastes capacity, so this RFC describes how a planning tool could consider both at once, and what it takes to build the missing links underneath.

questions: single pce vs multiple pce path computation
subtitle: How a Path Computation Element can plan routes across a packet layer and an optical layer at the same time.

tldr.problem: A network with several layers wastes capacity when each layer is optimised on its own, and a router in the upper layer often cannot see the lower layer well enough to compute a path across it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes three ways for Path Computation Elements to compute an end-to-end path across layers, and four ways to control the lower-layer links that make up the Virtual Network Topology.
tldr.outcome: It defines no protocol. It gives operators a table of which combinations work, and sets out the trade-offs in setup time, complexity, stability and policy separation.

facts.label: Mechanism for masking a lower-layer path

today: RFC 5623 is an Informational framework published in September 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines no protocol of its own: it sits inside the PCE architecture of RFC 4655 and describes how a path computation element and a virtual network topology manager could be arranged for multi-layer networks.

sections.title: Why Plan a Network Layer by Layer
sections.content:
A network may have several layers. The layers may separate technologies, such as packet switching, time division multiplexing and wavelength switching, or separate levels of switching granularity, or separate client and server roles. In such a network, Label Switched Paths (LSPs) in a lower layer carry higher-layer LSPs across the lower-layer network. The topology formed by those lower-layer LSPs, advertised in the higher layer as traffic engineering links, is called the Virtual Network Topology (VNT).

Optimising each layer on its own wastes resources. Optimising across all layers at once is called inter-layer traffic engineering. It has two halves: computing end-to-end paths across the layers, and controlling the VNT by setting up and releasing lower-layer LSPs.

RFC 5623 applies the Path Computation Element (PCE) architecture of RFC 4655 to this job. It defines no protocol. Instead it describes three models for computing paths across layers, four models for controlling the lower layer, the ways those models can be combined, and what each combination costs in setup time, complexity and administrative separation. The requirements for the PCE Communication Protocol are set out in a separate document.
sections.plainLanguage: Big networks are built in layers, and planning each layer on its own wastes capacity. This RFC describes how a planning tool could consider both at once.

sections.title: Computing a Path Across Two Layers
sections.content:
The RFC's running example is a two-layer network. The higher layer holds LSRs H1, H2, H3 and H4 in a packet-based IP/MPLS or GMPLS network. The lower layer holds H2, L1, L2 and H3 in a GMPLS optical network. H1 wants an LSP to H4 across the lower layer, but there is no TE link in the higher layer between the two border LSRs H2 and H3, and H1 has no topology visibility into the lower layer. A single-layer computation fails on the missing link; an inter-layer computation can return the route H1-H2-H3-H4 and suggest that a lower-layer LSP H2-L1-L2-H3 be set up.

The path the PCE returns reaches the head-end LSR as an Explicit Route Object (ERO) for RSVP-TE signaling, and it comes in two shapes. A mono-layer path uses TE links from one layer only. It may include lower-layer LSPs that already exist, lower-layer LSPs that do not exist yet and whose setup the signaling triggers, or a loose hop across the lower layer that a border LSR expands itself or with a PCE. A multi-layer path includes TE links from different layers and may name the complete route of lower-layer LSPs, existing or not yet established, in which case the higher-layer signaling triggers their setup.

The RFC also notes that a network with more than two layers, such as MPLS over SONET over an Optical Transport Network, can combine models: the single PCE model across the SONET and OTN layers, and the multiple PCE model with inter-PCE communication across the MPLS and SONET layers.
sections.plainLanguage: In the example, the router at one end cannot see the optical layer, and the link across it does not exist yet. The planner answers with the route through the upper layer and suggests which optical path to build underneath.

sections.title: Three Models for Computing the Path
sections.content:
Three models come from the PCE architecture.

Single PCE. One multi-layer PCE has topology visibility into all layers and computes the whole path itself, for example H1-H2-L1-L2-H3-H4. The RFC notes that this may be faster than the cooperative model, because there is no requirement to exchange messages between cooperating PCEs, and that the model suits a case where the topology of all layers is visible within one routing domain. The cost is computation power and memory, because the PCE holds and uses more topology information in a single computation.

Multiple PCE with inter-PCE communication. There is at least one PCE per layer, and each has visibility restricted to its own layer. The simple cooperation the RFC describes runs like this: LSR H1 asks PCE Hi for a path to H4; PCE Hi picks H2 as the entry point to the lower layer and H3 as the exit point; PCE Hi asks PCE Lo for a path from H2 to H3; PCE Lo returns H2-L1-L2-H3; PCE Hi returns the full path H1-H2-L1-L2-H3-H4 to H1. Providers may want this model to keep layer boundaries for organisational or service-management reasons, and it keeps the traffic engineering database of each PCE smaller.

Multiple PCE without inter-PCE communication. Separate computations are performed on behalf of the head-end LSR and of each transit border LSR that is the entry point to a new layer, each using its own per-layer path computation.

When the higher layer is multi-homed, optimal computation requires examining every path through every candidate border node. That is relatively simple in the single PCE model, where the computation resembles one inside a single domain of a single layer. With cooperating PCEs, the backward-recursive techniques of RFC 5441 could be used by considering the layers as separate domains.
sections.plainLanguage: You can have one planner that knows every layer, or one planner per layer who talk to each other, or one planner per layer who each work out their own part.

sections.title: Controlling the Lower Layer with a VNT Manager
sections.content:
Computing a path is only half the job. The VNT has to be controlled too, with lower-layer LSPs set up, changed and released to match what the higher layer needs. The RFC defines a Virtual Network Topology Manager (VNTM) as the functional element that manages and controls the VNT. The PCE and the VNTM are distinct elements that may or may not be collocated, and four path control models either use it or avoid it.

PCE-VNTM cooperation. The PCE tries to compute a path and fails for lack of a TE link between H2 and H3. It then suggests to the VNTM that a lower-layer LSP from H2 to H3 would be useful, telling the VNTM about the higher-layer demand and possibly including a suggested lower-layer route. The VNTM applies local policy and management input, and may ask an ingress LSR such as H2 to establish the lower-layer LSP. H2 then advertises the new LSP as a TE link in the higher layer, and the PCE recomputes and replies to H1. The RFC spells this out in ten steps and notes that if the PCE decides to wait it must operate a timeout, and that the path computation client has to understand that it may be kept waiting for some time.

Higher-layer signaling trigger. No VNTM is involved. The PCE returns either a multi-layer path such as H1-H2-L1-L2-H3-H4 or a mono-layer path with a loose hop such as H1-H2-H3(loose)-H4. When the higher-layer signaling message reaches border LSR H2, that router notices the next hop is in the lower layer and starts the lower-layer signaling itself, after checking local policy. With a loose hop, H2 has greater freedom to choose which lower-layer LSP to use, and it may also find that a suitable LSP has become available in the meantime and use that instead.

NMS-VNTM cooperation, integrated flavor. The network management system asks the PCE to compute, then works with the VNTM to have the lower-layer LSP set up. The VNTM and the NMS are closely coupled, and multiple PCE computation without inter-PCE communication does not fit this model.

NMS-VNTM cooperation, separate flavor. The NMS asks the head-end LSR to set up the higher-layer LSP without specifying a route; the PCE fails; the head-end notifies the NMS; the NMS asks the VNTM for a lower-layer LSP; the VNTM asks the lower-layer PCE for a path and asks H2 to set the LSP up; H2 advertises it and the NMS retries the request. The NMS-to-VNTM conversation may be automatic or manual, and is a natural place to apply administrative, billing and security policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone has to build the missing optical path. This RFC offers four ways to arrange that: a planner tells a manager, the router builds it when the request arrives, or the network management office sorts it out, closely or loosely coupled with the lower-layer manager.

sections.title: Choosing a Model and Keeping the Network Stable
sections.content:
Table 1 of the RFC lists which computation and control models can be combined. The PCE-VNTM and higher-layer signaling trigger models work with all three computation models. The integrated NMS-VNTM flavor does not fit multiple PCE computation without inter-PCE communication, and the separate flavor fits only that model; in the single PCE case with the separate flavor, the PCE function used by the NMS and the VNTM may be collocated, but it will operate on separate traffic engineering databases.

Choosing between the control models comes down to four things. VNTM functions. The VNTM is required by both cooperation models, and the higher-layer signaling trigger model requires no VNTM at all, so a network that does not have one has to use the trigger model. Having a VNTM also allows better coordination of cross-network LSP tunnels and of network-wide policy, which is far harder to apply in the trigger model because it requires coordinating policy between multiple border LSRs. Border LSR functions. The trigger model needs the border LSR to trigger lower-layer signaling and to expand a loose hop, either by consulting a PCE or with its own computation engine. The cooperation models need no such extra function, except where virtual TE links are used. Setup time. The cooperation models add communication steps between the path computation client and the PCE, the PCE and the VNTM, the NMS and the VNTM, and the VNTM and the LSR, so they give better control at the cost of a longer setup time. In the trigger model the higher-layer signaling itself takes longer, because the lower-layer signaling has to take place during it. Network complexity. With several interconnects between the layers, the higher-layer LSP must be routed to the correct border nodes for both layers to be optimal, and the cost metrics and shared risk link groups of the advertised lower-layer LSPs need care.

Stability is the RFC's main operational warning. Lower-layer LSPs tend to have considerably higher capacity than higher-layer ones, so a very large LSP may be established in support of a very small traffic demand, and if the higher-layer LSP is short-lived the lower-layer one is either left in place but unused or has to be torn down. Worse, a new lower-layer LSP can attract existing higher-layer LSPs, whose departure then under-utilises other lower-layer LSPs, which are deleted once their utilisation drops below a threshold, which in turn makes room for the next request. The RFC asks that operators have policy controls or configuration features so that demand-led establishment of lower-layer LSPs, what it calls bandwidth on demand, is filtered according to the requirements of the lower-layer network, and that threshold parameters give hysteresis control over re-routing and deletion.

Manageability follows the same lines. PCEs that support inter-layer computation should have a configuration switch to enable or disable it, and each layer may have its own policy or the operator may keep a single integrated policy across all of them. Inter-layer policy should define the points of connectivity between the layers, the model to apply, and the rules for path computation and LSP setup, and it should reach the PCEs that do the computation. A VNTM is a natural place to hold that policy, because it lets the lower-layer administrator apply it without making it public to the higher-layer operator.
sections.plainLanguage: Which arrangement to use depends on who runs what and how fast a path has to appear. The RFC also warns against building a huge optical path for one small request and tearing it down again, because that cycle can make the whole network flap.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Inter-layer traffic engineering with a PCE raises security issues in all of the path control models.

In the PCE-VNTM model, the communications between the PCE and the VNTM and between the VNTM and the border LSR should carry authenticity, privacy and integrity protections. The RFC is explicit about why: a false trigger for lower-layer LSP setup could tie up lower-layer resources, which amounts to a denial-of-service attack on the lower layer and on the higher layer trying to use it, and could produce incorrect billing for services the lower layer provides. Where the PCE MIB modules carry the notifications between the higher-layer PCE and the VNTM, SNMPv3 should be used, and the VNTM should have configurable or dynamic policy functions so that its reaction to a notification can be controlled.

In the higher-layer signaling trigger model the main concern is confidentiality. The PCE may tell a higher-layer path computation client about a path that includes lower-layer hops, but the client may have no TE topology visibility into the lower layer and might not be trusted with that information. A loose hop across the lower layer hides the route but decreases the benefit of multi-layer traffic engineering. A better alternative is to mask the lower-layer path using a path key from RFC 5520, which can be expanded within the lower-layer network. The recorded lower-layer path information should also be filtered, and the security of signaling at the inter-layer interface needs attention because the layers may belong to different administrative or trust domains.

The NMS-VNTM model moves the issue into the management plane, where the RFC treats the NMS-to-VNTM communication as out of scope. It notes that the model may address many security and policy concerns, because the control and the decision-making are placed within the sphere of influence of the operator, in contrast to the more dynamic mechanisms of the other models, but that the security issues have simply moved and will require authentication of operators and of policy.

One risk comes from the single PCE model itself. Any access to a PCE with full visibility of TE information for several layers immediately gives access to the topology of every layer, so a single security breach exposes information that would take multiple breaches to reach in the other models. Finally, the RFC notes that the instability described earlier could itself be leveraged to attack either the higher or the lower layer, and that the precautionary policy controls of the manageability section can dampen such oscillation.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever can fake a request to build an optical path could waste the operator's resources or falsify its billing. A planner that sees every layer is also a single point of failure for the whole map.
